tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

91	|---|---|---|
92	| File missing/unreadable | 3 / 4 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
93	| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 / 4 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |

102	| Bad priority | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid priority '<value>'` |

Use the shared [workflow terminology](../../AGENTS.md#workflow-terminology).

# Spec Research & Authoring

Deploy a parallel research team to investigate requirements for a new spec, then synthesize findings into a complete feature specification document. The research phase uses 3 subagents with distinct investigation angles to ensure comprehensive coverage before writing begins.

## Arguments

Accept a spec topic or folder path (e.g., `notifications`, `feature-007`, `docs/notifications/`, or a plain description like "real-time notifications system").  
If a stub README already exists in the feature folder (for example `docs/feature-name/README.md`), read it for initial scope constraints.

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Scope Discovery

Before dispatching researchers:

1. Determine the feature folder name. If the argument is already a folder path, use it. Otherwise derive `docs/spec-NNN-<kebab-slug>/`: read `CLAUDE.md` `## Current State` for the current sequence if present. If `CLAUDE.md` is missing, malformed, or the `## Current State` section is absent, continue with fallback naming logic: list existing `docs/spec-*` folders and use the highest number + 1. If no numbered folders exist, follow whatever folder convention prior specs in `docs/` use; if `docs/` is empty, ask the user to confirm the folder name before proceeding.
2. Read any existing stub (`docs/<folder>/README.md`) for scope constraints.
3. Scan the codebase for existing patterns and integration points.
4. Identify 3 distinct research angles based on what the feature needs to cover.

### Phase 2: Define 3 Research Angles

Select 3 non-overlapping research angles based on the feature domain. Each agent investigates a different facet.

Typical per-domain configurations (infrastructure / domain-feature / security-compliance, always anchored by a Codebase Analyst) are in `references/research-angle-menus.md` — load it when picking the angles.

### Phase 3: Dispatch Research Team in Parallel

Deploy all 3 researchers simultaneously.

- **Codebase Analyst**: use `geeky-orchestration:code-explorer` agent type.
- **Web Researchers (2)**: use `general-purpose` agent type with instructions to use `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`.

Each research brief ends with:

```
Produce a structured report with:
- Key findings (numbered, specific)
- Constraints discovered (what the spec MUST respect)
- Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)
- Sources (URLs for web research, file paths for codebase)

DO NOT create or modify any files.
```

### Phase 4: Synthesize into Spec Document

After all 3 researchers report back:

1. Consolidate findings: merge overlap, resolve contradictions, and note confidence gaps.
2. Define scope: goals, non-goals, delegation items.
3. Write the requirements document using the project’s established conventions in:
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/feature-specification.md`
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/README.md`

   Do not create `SPEC-NNNN-*.md` files — that naming is legacy; `feature-specification.md` is the canonical filename consumed by /geeky-plan and the freeze hooks.

   If a stub README already exists, preserve its stated scope and only update the Status line and missing sections; otherwise create the README stub:

   ```markdown
   # [Feature Name]

   [One-paragraph scope summary.]

   **Status:** Spec written — not yet planned
   **Spec:** `feature-specification.md`
   **Next:** /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/
   ```

Use the 11-section recommended spec structure in `references/spec-structure-template.md` (adapt sections to the feature domain; include citations and explicit assumptions at the end of major findings).

### Phase 5: Commit and Suggest Next Steps

Commit the spec (same command on all platforms). The spec is not yet frozen — it only becomes part of the frozen planning contract after /geeky-plan runs:

```
git add docs/<feature-folder>/
git commit -m "docs: author feature specification in <feature-folder>" -m "[1-line summary of the spec focus]" -m "Research conducted by: codebase analyst, researcher 2 domain, researcher 3 domain"
```

Then suggest next steps:
```
Spec written. Next steps:
- /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/   (to create implementation plan, tasks, kanban)
- /plan-review docs/<feature-folder>/  (to validate the planning package)
- /geeky-implement docs/<feature-folder>/ (to execute)
```

## Research Quality Standards

- **Recency**: Target sources from roughly the past 18 months; avoid older sources unless they cover stable fundamentals.
- **Authority**: Prefer official documentation (Microsoft Learn, AWS docs, RFC specs) over blogs or forums.
- **Specificity**: Include concrete findings (resource types, API versions, package versions, pricing tiers).
- **Adversarial verification**: If researchers disagree on a fact, preserve both positions and flag for user decision.

## Rules

- **Always 3 researchers** — one codebase analyst + two web/domain researchers.
- **Parallel dispatch** — all 3 in a single turn for maximum speed.
- **Research before writing** — do not start the spec document until all researchers report back.
- **Cite sources** — every major claim in the spec should trace to research.
- **Respect existing stubs** — if a README stub exists, treat its stated scope as authoritative unless research justifies adjustments.
- **Follow project conventions** — spec format, naming, and folder structure should match prior specs in `docs/`.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

1	Build `csvledger`, a small Python command-line tool that reads one or more bank-export CSV files of transactions, assigns each transaction a category using a rules file, and prints a monthly report. It must run as `python -m csvledger` from the repository root using only the Python 3.11+ standard library. Provide two commands: `report` (per-month, per-category totals) and `categorize` (each transaction with its assigned category). Both commands print either an aligned text table or JSON. Money must be exact (no floating point) and output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback. Identical transactions repeated across overlapping exports must be counted once. The full interface contract is in `contract.md`; include pytest tests for your implementation.
2

1	# csvledger: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `csvledger/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
7	- **Entry point:** `python -m csvledger <command> ...` run from repo root.
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1** `python -m csvledger` exposes subcommands `report` and `categorize`; `--help` exits 0.
12	- **R2** Transaction files are parsed per the CSV contract; any invalid file or row aborts the run with exit 3 and no stdout.
13	- **R3** The rules file is parsed per the rules contract; any invalid rule aborts with exit 4 and no stdout.
14	- **R4** Each transaction gets exactly one category: the highest-priority matching rule; ties go to the rule earliest in the file; no match gives `Uncategorized`.
15	- **R5** Duplicate transactions (same date, stripped description, and numeric amount value) across all inputs are kept once (first occurrence) and a warning is written to stderr. Deduplication runs over all rows of all input files before the `--month` filter; the warning count N covers duplicates across all inputs regardless of `--month`.
16	- **R6** `report` aggregates by month and category: count, income, expenses, net.
17	- **R7** `categorize` lists every transaction, sorted by date ascending, ties in input order.
18	- **R8** `--month YYYY-MM` restricts both commands to transactions in that month.
19	- **R9** `--format table|json` selects output; default `table`.
20	- **R10** Money uses `decimal.Decimal`; sums are exact; displayed values are rounded once to 2 dp, ROUND_HALF_UP, never shown as `-0.00`.
21	- **R11** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, stable ordering, no locale use.
22	
23	## Interface contract
24	
25	### Commands
26	
27	```
28	python -m csvledger report     [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
29	python -m csvledger categorize [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
30	```
31	
32	- `FILE`: one or more transaction CSV paths, processed in argument order. `-` is an ordinary file name; stdin is never read.
33	- `--rules`: optional. When omitted, every transaction is `Uncategorized`.
34	- `--month`: must match `^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$`, else usage error.
35	- argparse `prog` is `csvledger`. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
36	- Load order: rules file first, then transaction files in argument order. First error wins.
37	
38	### Exit codes
39	
40	| Code | Meaning |
41	|---|---|
42	| 0 | Success (including empty result and duplicate warnings) |
43	| 1 | Reserved for unexpected internal error; never intentional |
44	| 2 | Usage error (argparse: unknown flag, missing FILE, bad `--format`/`--month`) |
45	| 3 | Transaction file error |
46	| 4 | Rules file error |
47	
48	### Transaction CSV
49	
50	- Encoding UTF-8, optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`); opened with `newline=""`; parsed with `csv.reader` defaults (comma, `"` quoting).
51	- Line 1 is the header. Header names are stripped and lowercased; `date`, `description`, `amount` are required, in any order; extra columns are ignored; duplicate names are an error.
52	- Rows with zero fields (blank lines) are skipped. Every other row must have exactly as many fields as the header.
53	- `date`: stripped value must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a valid calendar date (regex first; do not rely on `date.fromisoformat` alone).
54	- `amount`: stripped value must match `^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$`. Negative = expense (outflow), positive = income, zero counts but adds to neither.
55	- `description`: stripped; may be empty.
56	- A header-only file is valid (zero transactions). A file with no header line (0 bytes) is an error.
57	
58	### Rules CSV
59	
60	- Same encoding/header/blank-row/field-count rules. Required columns: `category`, `type`, `pattern`, `priority`.
61	- `category`: stripped, non-empty. `type`: stripped, exactly `contains` or `regex`. `pattern`: stripped, non-empty. `priority`: stripped, matches `^-?\d+$`.
62	- `contains`: `pattern.casefold() in description.casefold()`.
63	- `regex`: `re.search(pattern, description, re.IGNORECASE)`; compiled at load time.
64	- Zero rules is valid.
65	
66	### Money formatting
67	
68	`q = value.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), ROUND_HALF_UP)`; if `q == 0` print `0.00`; otherwise `format(q, "f")`. Aggregates (income, expenses, net, month totals) are summed unrounded, then formatted. `net = income_raw + expenses_raw`.
69	
70	### `report` table
71	
72	Columns, in order: `MONTH` (left), `CATEGORY` (left), `COUNT` (right), `INCOME` (right), `EXPENSES` (right), `NET` (right). Width of each column = max(len(header), longest value) using `len()` on code points. Cells joined by two spaces; each line right-stripped. Line 1: headers. Line 2: dashes of each column width. Then one row per (month, category), sorted by month ascending then category by code-point ascending. No total rows. Zero transactions: header and dash line only.
73	
74	### `categorize` table
75	
76	Columns: `DATE` (left), `AMOUNT` (right, per-transaction amount formatted as money), `CATEGORY` (left), `DESCRIPTION` (left). Same width, separator, dash-line and right-strip rules.
77	
78	### JSON
79	
80	`json.dumps(obj, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` followed by `\n`. Money values are strings; counts are integers. Key order is exactly as shown.
81	
82	- `report`: `{"months": [{"month", "count", "income", "expenses", "net", "categories": [{"category", "count", "income", "expenses", "net"}]}]}`. Months and categories sorted as in the table.
83	- `categorize`: `{"transactions": [{"date", "description", "amount", "category"}]}`.
84	- Empty: `{"months": []}` / `{"transactions": []}`.
85	
86	## Error handling
87	
88	Errors go to stderr as one line, prefix `csvledger: error: `, then exit with the code shown; stdout stays empty. `<path>` is exactly the argv string given on the command line (a relative path stays relative); `<line>` is `csv.reader.line_num` after reading the record. Row checks run in this order: field count, date, amount (transactions) or field count, category, type, pattern, priority, regex (rules). Header checks run in this order: (1) no header line, (2) duplicate column, (3) missing required column. For a duplicate column, `<name>` is the second occurrence after strip and lowercase, and the first duplicate in header order is reported. For a missing column, `<name>` is the first absent name in the listed order.
89	
90	| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
91	|---|---|---|
92	| File missing/unreadable | 3 / 4 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
93	| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 / 4 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
94	| No header line | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing header` |
95	| Duplicate header name (first duplicate in header order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: duplicate column '<name>'` |
96	| Required column absent (first in listed order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing column '<name>'` |
97	| Field count mismatch | 3 / 4 | `<path>:<line>: expected <N> fields, got <M>` |
98	| Bad date | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid date '<value>'` |
99	| Bad amount | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid amount '<value>'` |
100	| Empty category / pattern | 4 | `<path>:<line>: empty category` / `empty pattern` |
101	| Bad type | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid type '<value>'` |
102	| Bad priority | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid priority '<value>'` |
103	| Regex fails to compile | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid regex '<pattern>'` |
104	| argparse usage errors | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match the regex `^csvledger( report\| categorize)?: error: ` (argparse subparser prog form allowed) |
105	
106	Warning (exit unaffected): `csvledger: warning: skipped <N> duplicate row(s)` when N > 0, written after stdout output. `<value>` is the stripped field value.
107	
108	## Acceptance criteria
109	
110	- **AC1 (R1)** `python -m csvledger --help` → exit 0, stdout mentions `report` and `categorize`.
111	- **AC2 (R2, R3, R4, R6, R9, R10)** Oracle case O1 → stdout equals the O1 table exactly, exit 0.
112	- **AC3 (R6, R9)** `report --format json` on O1 input → valid JSON with key order per contract; January Groceries `expenses` is `"-57.11"`.
113	- **AC4 (R7)** `categorize` on O1 input → rows in date order; `Blue Bottle Cafe` categorized `Coffee`.
114	- **AC5 (R8)** `report --month 2026-02` on O1 input → only `2026-02` rows.
115	- **AC6 (R5)** O4 → each duplicated row counted once; stderr warning; exit 0.
116	- **AC7 (R2)** O3 → exit 3, exact stderr line, empty stdout.
117	- **AC8 (R3)** Invalid regex rule → exit 4, `invalid regex` message.
118	- **AC9 (R10)** O5 → `0.13`, `-0.13`, `0.00`, `0.01` as shown.
119	- **AC10 (R11)** Running any case twice yields identical bytes; output contains no `\r`.
120	
121	### Cases referenced by the acceptance criteria
122	
123	File contents below are exact; each line ends with `\n`.
124	
125	**O1.** `rules.csv`:
126	```
127	category,type,pattern,priority
128	Groceries,contains,market,10
129	Coffee,regex,^(starbucks|blue bottle),10
130	Dining,contains,cafe,5
131	Salary,contains,payroll,0
132	```
133	`tx.csv`:
134	```
135	date,description,amount
136	2026-01-03,Corner Market,-45.10
137	2026-01-05,STARBUCKS #12,-4.50
138	2026-01-15,ACME PAYROLL,2500.00
139	2026-01-20,Corner Market,-12.005
140	2026-02-02,Blue Bottle Cafe,-6.25
141	2026-02-10,Unknown Shop,-10
142	```
143	`report --rules rules.csv tx.csv` → exit 0, stdout:
144	```
145	MONTH    CATEGORY       COUNT   INCOME  EXPENSES      NET
146	-------  -------------  -----  -------  --------  -------
147	2026-01  Coffee             1     0.00     -4.50    -4.50
148	2026-01  Groceries          2     0.00    -57.11   -57.11
149	2026-01  Salary             1  2500.00      0.00  2500.00
150	2026-02  Coffee             1     0.00     -6.25    -6.25
151	2026-02  Uncategorized      1     0.00    -10.00   -10.00
152	```
153	
154	**O3.** `tx.csv`:
155	```
156	date,description,amount
157	2026-02-01,Y,-1
158	2026-02-30,X,-1
159	```
160	`report tx.csv` → exit 3, empty stdout, stderr `csvledger: error: tx.csv:3: invalid date '2026-02-30'`.
161	
162	**O4.** `rules.csv` as in O1. `a.csv`:
163	```
164	date,description,amount
165	2026-01-05,STARBUCKS #12,-4.50
166	```
167	`b.csv` (the description has two spaces on each side):
168	```
169	date,description,amount

171	```
172	`report --rules rules.csv a.csv b.csv` → exit 0, one `2026-01  Coffee` row with count 1 and expenses `-4.50`; stderr `csvledger: warning: skipped 1 duplicate row(s)`.
173

Use the shared [workflow terminology](../../AGENTS.md#workflow-terminology).

# Spec Research & Authoring

Deploy a parallel research team to investigate requirements for a new spec, then synthesize findings into a complete feature specification document. The research phase uses 3 subagents with distinct investigation angles to ensure comprehensive coverage before writing begins.

## Arguments

Accept a spec topic or folder path (e.g., `notifications`, `feature-007`, `docs/notifications/`, or a plain description like "real-time notifications system").  
If a stub README already exists in the feature folder (for example `docs/feature-name/README.md`), read it for initial scope constraints.

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Scope Discovery

Before dispatching researchers:

1. Determine the feature folder name. If the argument is already a folder path, use it. Otherwise derive `docs/spec-NNN-<kebab-slug>/`: read `CLAUDE.md` `## Current State` for the current sequence if present. If `CLAUDE.md` is missing, malformed, or the `## Current State` section is absent, continue with fallback naming logic: list existing `docs/spec-*` folders and use the highest number + 1. If no numbered folders exist, follow whatever folder convention prior specs in `docs/` use; if `docs/` is empty, ask the user to confirm the folder name before proceeding.
2. Read any existing stub (`docs/<folder>/README.md`) for scope constraints.
3. Scan the codebase for existing patterns and integration points.
4. Identify 3 distinct research angles based on what the feature needs to cover.

### Phase 2: Define 3 Research Angles

Select 3 non-overlapping research angles based on the feature domain. Each agent investigates a different facet.

Typical per-domain configurations (infrastructure / domain-feature / security-compliance, always anchored by a Codebase Analyst) are in `references/research-angle-menus.md` — load it when picking the angles.

### Phase 3: Dispatch Research Team in Parallel

Deploy all 3 researchers simultaneously.

- **Codebase Analyst**: use `geeky-orchestration:code-explorer` agent type.
- **Web Researchers (2)**: use `general-purpose` agent type with instructions to use `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`.

Each research brief ends with:

```
Produce a structured report with:
- Key findings (numbered, specific)
- Constraints discovered (what the spec MUST respect)
- Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)
- Sources (URLs for web research, file paths for codebase)

DO NOT create or modify any files.
```

### Phase 4: Synthesize into Spec Document

After all 3 researchers report back:

1. Consolidate findings: merge overlap, resolve contradictions, and note confidence gaps.
2. Define scope: goals, non-goals, delegation items.
3. Write the requirements document using the project’s established conventions in:
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/feature-specification.md`
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/README.md`

Every finding comes from the two spec files, plus my knowledge of the Python standard library (`csv`, `decimal`, `argparse`, `re`, `io`) that I did not check against a running interpreter or the docs.

## What exists
- The repo holds `brief.md`, `contract.md` and `.gitignore`, plus the git history. The only commit is `ee3261e seed: brief and contract`.

   - `csvio.py`: shared reader, which opens the file with `utf-8-sig` and `newline=""`, runs the header checks, skips blank rows, and checks field count.
   - `transactions.py`: date and amount validation, `Transaction` dataclass.
   - `rules.py`: rule parsing, regex compilation, matching, `categorize()`.
   - `dedupe.py`
   - `aggregate.py`
   - `formatting.py`: `fmt_money`, table rendering and JSON rendering.
2. The shared reader is the main reuse point. Transaction and rules files share the encoding, header, blank-row and field-count rules. They differ only in required columns, exit code and per-row checks.
3. The data flow is: rules, then each transaction file in argv order, then dedupe over all rows, then the `--month` filter, then categorize, then aggregate or sort, then format, then write stdout, then the stderr warning.
4. Whether to categorize before or after dedupe is not observable, because dedupe keys do not include category. I would categorize after the month filter.
5. The integration points are only the stdlib: `argparse`, `csv`, `decimal`, `re`, `json`, `sys`, `datetime`. There are no external services.

6. **Dedupe "numeric amount value" versus string.** The key must be `(date_str, stripped_description, Decimal)`.
   - `Decimal("4.50") == Decimal("4.5")` and the hashes are equal, so a dict or set works.
   - `Decimal("-0")` and `Decimal("0.00")` are equal, so `-0.00` and `0` duplicate each other.
   - Do not key on `as_tuple()` or on the string.
   - The date is compared as the stripped string. That is safe because it is zero-padded and already validated.
7. **Dedupe scope.** R5 says "across all inputs", so duplicates inside a single file also collapse. Two genuine identical purchases on one day are then merged. The contract is explicit about this, but it is surprising and the spec should say so outright. It also means the same file passed twice is entirely duplicates.
8. **`-0.00` handling.**
   - The amount regex accepts `-0`, `-0.00` and `-0.000`.
   - "Zero counts but adds to neither" must be tested by sign, with `> 0` for income and `< 0` for expenses. `Decimal('-0') < 0` is False, so that works.

   - JSON `amount` strings in `categorize` go through the same formatter.
9. **Sorting.**
   - Categories sort by code-point, which is Python's default `str` order. Do not use `locale` or `casefold`.
   - Months sort as ISO strings.
   - `categorize` needs a stable sort on the date only. Input order means argv file order, then row order, after dedupe.
   - "Ties to the rule earliest in the file" combined with priority needs `max` by `(priority, -index)`, or a stable sort descending on priority.
   - Higher priority number wins. The contract implies this but never says it. Negatives are allowed.

    - `csv.reader.line_num` counts physical lines consumed, so a record with embedded newlines reports its last line.
    - Blank lines and the header line are counted.
    - The contract says "after reading the record", which matches this. The spec should state it explicitly and add a test.
11. **Warning versus stdout ordering.**

    - A duplicate warning must not appear if a later file produces an error, because dedupe only runs after all loads.

    - `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` is valid.
    - It fails if stdout is not a `TextIOWrapper`, for example under pytest `capsys`. Guard it with `hasattr` or a try/except.
    - Stderr is not covered by the contract. On Windows it uses the console code page, so a non-encodable path or value in an error message raises `UnicodeEncodeError`, which is a traceback.
    - Stderr also writes `\r\n` on Windows by default, which conflicts with "one line" tests.
    - I recommend reconfiguring stderr the same way.

    - Under `-m`, `sys.argv[0]` is `__main__.py`, so `prog="csvledger"` is required.
    - Subparsers then get the prog `csvledger report` and `csvledger categorize`, which the stderr regex permits.

    - `^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$` has two defects:

16. **Money exactness versus the default decimal context.**
    - Decimal arithmetic uses the default context of 28 significant digits, so large sums or long amounts round silently.

22. **Dash line and cells.** Cells are joined by two spaces, and the dash line is built from the column widths, before the right-strip.
23. **Empty JSON output.** `json.dumps({"months": []}, indent=2)` gives `{\n  "months": []\n}`, followed by `\n`.
24. **JSON month count.** The month `count` is the sum of its category counts. The contract does not say so, but it is the only sensible reading.

    - Usage errors (exit 2) come before either.
    - Within a file, row order decides.

8. Require `subparsers.required = True`, so a bare invocation exits 2.
9. Require a top-level catch for `csv.Error`, `UnicodeDecodeError`, `OSError` and `ValueError`, mapped to the specified messages. Add an "internal error" fallback with exit 1.
10. Reconfigure stderr to UTF-8 with `\n` line endings, or at least with `errors="backslashreplace"`.
11. Write output once: build a string, write it, flush stdout, then emit the warning.
12. State explicitly that the output ends with a trailing `\n` after the last table row.

    - Put tests in `tests/` at the repo root, with `conftest.py` providing a `run(args, cwd)` fixture that calls `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "csvledger", ...], cwd=repo_root, capture_output=True)` and compares **bytes**, since text mode would translate newlines. Add a smaller set of in-process `main(argv)` tests for speed.

Additional test cases beyond the oracles: UTF-8 BOM, a header-only file, a 0-byte file, a quoted multiline description, a file with only blank lines, a rules file with zero rules, and a regex rule that fails to compile at line 3. <result># Research report: Python behaviors relevant to the csvledger spec

I ran experiments on CPython 3.13.15 with `python -I`, then checked the official docs.python.org pages. I created no files. The behaviors below come from 3.13. The 3.11 docs say the same for these features, except the points I flag.

## Key findings

1. **csv and the BOM.** `open(p, encoding='utf-8', newline='')` leaves the BOM in the first header cell, giving `'\ufeffDate'`. With `encoding='utf-8-sig'` the cell is `'Date'`. The csv docs never mention the BOM, so handling it is the caller's job.
2. **`newline=''`.** The docs say a file object "should be opened with `newline=''`", and that without it embedded newlines in quoted fields are not interpreted correctly. The module does its own universal newline handling.
3. **`line_num` counts physical lines.** It is "the number of lines read from the source iterator", not records.
   - Test input: `a,b`, a blank line, a quoted field spanning two lines, a whitespace-only line, then `,`.
   - Row-by-row output (line_num, row): `1 ['a','b']`, `2 []`, `4 ['x\ny','2']`, `5 ['   ']`, `6 ['','']`.
   - `line_num` is the line where the record ended, not where it started. A multiline record reports its last line.
   - A record's start line is the previous `line_num` + 1, but only if the previous record was not blank. Tracking the start line takes extra bookkeeping.
4. **Blank rows.** A truly empty line yields `[]`. A whitespace-only line yields `['   ']`, a one-element list that is not empty. A line of only commas yields `['', '']`. The docs do not specify the `[]` behavior; I confirmed it empirically.
5. **Lazy decode errors.** `UnicodeDecodeError` surfaces mid-iteration, not at `open()`.
   - A file with an invalid byte after about 5000 valid rows opened fine, the header read fine, and the error was raised at `line_num` 4096.
   - Text files decode in chunks, so the reported `line_num` is the last line of the previous chunk. It does not point at the bad line.
   - The spec should wrap the whole read loop, not just `open()`. It cannot promise an exact line number for decode errors.
6. **`Decimal.quantize` with `ROUND_HALF_UP`.** The docs define it as "ties going away from zero".
   - `2.675` becomes `2.68`.
   - `-2.675` becomes `-2.68`.
   - `-0.005` becomes `-0.01`.
   - `quantize` raises `InvalidOperation` if the coefficient would exceed the context precision (default 28 digits). A huge amount therefore fails at quantize time.
7. **Negative zero survives quantize.** `Decimal('-0.001').quantize(Decimal('0.01'), ROUND_HALF_UP)` gives `Decimal('-0.00')`.
   - `format(q, 'f')` prints `-0.00`.

    - `'Straße'.casefold()` gives `'strasse'`, and `.lower()` keeps `ß`.

    - `'İ'.casefold()` gives `'i̇'` (i plus a combining dot, two code points).

- Skip blank rows with `if not row`. Decide whether whitespace-only or comma-only rows count as blank, and say so.

  - BOM header.
  - Blank line, whitespace-only line, and a quoted multiline field, with `line_num` assertions.
  - Mid-file invalid UTF-8.
  - `-0.00`, `-0.001`, `0.005`, `-0.005`, `2.675`.
  - `-4.50` versus `-4.5` duplicates.
  - Fullwidth and Arabic-Indic digits.
  - `12\n` in a field.
  - `20240105`, `2024-W01-1`, `2024-1-5`, and a datetime string for dates.
  - A casefold case such as `Straße`.
- Decide whether to strip header and cell whitespace (`str.strip`) and whether to use `skipinitialspace`. State the choice, and note that NBSP is removed by `strip` but a BOM is not.
- Decide whether to use `csv.Reader(strict=True)`. Strict mode makes malformed quoting an error. The default silently accepts it.

I read the official docs.python.org pages for argparse, io, json and cmdline. I also ran a probe script on this machine (CPython 3.13.15, Windows, `python -I -c`). I did not verify Windows console/pipe code-page behaviour or the 3.11 vs 3.14 argparse text differences by running them. Those items are marked "(knowledge, unverified)". I also did not run pytest, tmp_path or pipe-ordering experiments. Those parts are reasoned from documented behaviour and are marked as recommendations.

## Key findings

**argparse**
1. Under `python -m csvledger` the default `prog` is `__main__.py`, so `prog="csvledger"` must be passed explicitly. Subparsers then inherit `csvledger report` and `csvledger categorize` automatically. Probe output: `usage: csvledger report [-h] ... FILE [FILE ...]` and `csvledger report: error: ...`.
2. `add_subparsers(required=...)` defaults to False (docs). Without `required=True`, a bare `python -m csvledger` does not error. Pass `dest="command"` as well. The probe printed `csvledger: error: the following arguments are required: command` with exit 2 for the empty argv. Without `dest`, the missing-subcommand message and metavar are poor (knowledge, unverified).
3. Parse errors exit 2 and print usage plus `<prog>: error: <msg>` to stderr, and the error line is the last line. This is confirmed by the docs and the probe. The contract regex `^csvledger( report| categorize)?: error: ` matches the last line in every probed case: missing FILE, bad `--format`, unknown/extra args, and no subcommand.
4. `--help` exits 0 (standard argparse; the docs extract was truncated before that section, unverified by probe). Help goes to stdout, and the top-level usage line lists `{report,categorize}`, which satisfies AC1.
5. Do not use `argparse.FileType`, because it turns `-` into stdin or stdout and is deprecated in 3.14 (docs). Declare FILE with `nargs="+"`, `metavar="FILE"` and no `type`, so `-` stays a plain string. The probe returned `files=['-']`. A lone `-` is treated as a positional, not an option.
6. `nargs='+'` with no arguments gives `the following arguments are required: FILE` and exit 2 (docs, probe).
7. Interleaving fails. `report a --format json b` gives `csvledger: error: unrecognized arguments: b` with exit 2 (probe). Options must come before the FILE run or after all of it. The error text is reported by the top-level parser, as `csvledger:` rather than `csvledger report:`. The contract regex allows both. `parse_intermixed_args` is an option if the spec wants to accept this form.
8. `allow_abbrev` defaults to True. The probe accepted `--form json` as `--format`. The contract says unknown flag is exit 2 but is silent on prefixes. The spec should either allow or forbid them (`allow_abbrev=False`). Note that `allow_abbrev` is set per parser, so it must be passed to each subparser.
9. The `invalid choice` wording differs across Python versions. The probe on 3.13 printed `(choose from 'table', 'json')`. Tests must match only the `csvledger( report)?: error: ` prefix, not the full message.
10. `--month` should be validated with a `type=` callable that raises `argparse.ArgumentTypeError`. That gives exit 2 with `argument --month: ...`.
11. In 3.14, help can be colourised. Tests should not set `FORCE_COLOR`, and should clear it from the child env.

**Regex and number semantics that the contract's `\d` and `$` get wrong**
12. In a `str` pattern, `\d` matches any Unicode decimal digit. The probe matched the Arabic-Indic `٢٠٢٦-01` against the month regex. `Decimal("٢٣")` and `int("٢٣")` both succeed (probe printed 23 for each). Accepted non-ASCII digits would make amounts, dates and priorities pass validation, and these are not the intended input.
13. `$` also matches before a trailing newline. The probe matched `"2026-01\n"` with `re.match`. This matters for argv `--month`, which is not stripped.
14. The spec should require `re.fullmatch` with `[0-9]` (or `re.ASCII`) for month, date, amount and priority.

**Decimal exactness**
15. The default decimal context is prec=28. Construction from a string is exact, but `+` and `quantize` round or fail. The probe summed a 30-digit value and got `1.111111111111111111111111111E+29`. Quantizing it raised `InvalidOperation`. This would let a long amount produce a traceback or silently inexact sums, which violates R10 and "never a traceback". The spec should require a local context with large precision (for example `decimal.localcontext()` with `prec` well above the longest possible amount, or one derived from input length) and `Emax` set high enough.

**csv module**
16. `csv.reader` raises `csv.Error: field larger than field limit (131072)` (probe). It is not an `OSError` or `UnicodeDecodeError`, and the contract has no row for it. The spec should map it to exit 3 or 4 with a defined message, or raise the limit with `csv.field_size_limit`.
17. NUL bytes pass through: `a\x00b` was parsed as a field (probe, on 3.13; 3.11 behaviour unverified). Control characters can therefore reach the output.
18. `line_num` after reading a record that spans two physical lines is the last physical line (probe: 2 for a quoted newline in the second record). The spec should state that `<line>` means the physical line number at the end of the record.
19. `UnicodeDecodeError` surfaces lazily, during iteration of the reader, not at `open()`. The whole read loop must sit inside the `try`.
20. A blank first line is ambiguous. `csv.reader` returns `[]` for it, which the "zero fields are skipped" rule would skip, so the real header would be line 2. The spec must say whether a blank line 1 means "missing header" or is skipped.

**Output determinism**
21. `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` is valid (docs). It keeps the unspecified parameters, and giving `encoding` without `errors` resets `errors` to `'strict'`. It is allowed before any read, and it flushes first.
22. Default `newline=None` converts `\n` to `os.linesep` on write, which is `\r\n` on Windows. `newline=""` and `"\n"` do not translate (docs). This is why reconfiguring is required.
23. Under pytest `capsys`, `sys.stdout` is a replacement stream. Guard the reconfigure with `hasattr` or a try/except, and do it once at process entry rather than inside the library functions.
24. The most robust option is to build the whole output as one string, then write `text.encode("utf-8")` to `sys.stdout.buffer` in one call, followed by `flush()`. That avoids newline translation and encoder surprises entirely. It also guarantees "no stdout on error".
25. `json.dumps(obj, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` uses separators `(',', ': ')` and has no trailing whitespace (docs). The probe showed three details the contract leaves loose:
    - Empty results are three lines, not the one line shown in the contract: `'{\n  "months": []\n}'`, plus the `\n` the contract appends.
    - With `ensure_ascii=False`, control characters U+0000 to U+001F are escaped (`\u0000`, `\u001f`, `\n`).
    - `\x7f`, U+2028 and lone surrogates are emitted raw.
26. A raw lone surrogate makes the later UTF-8 encode raise `UnicodeEncodeError`. It cannot come from strict-decoded files. It can only come from argv paths on POSIX (surrogateescape), and paths never appear in the JSON output.
27. Table cells can contain `\n`, `\r` or other control characters (description fields from quoted CSV values). The contract is silent. A `\r` or `\n` inside a cell breaks the "each line" layout and can violate AC10 ("no `\r`"). The spec must say whether table output escapes or replaces these characters, or whether the rows are emitted verbatim. JSON is safe because json escapes them.
28. `str.rstrip()` with no argument strips Unicode whitespace, not just spaces. For "each line right-stripped" the spec should say which it means. Descriptions are already `strip()`ped, so the practical risk is low.

**Environment independence**
29. `PYTHONIOENCODING` overrides the encoding for stdin, stdout and stderr (docs). The stderr error handler is always `backslashreplace`. Redirected pipes are not affected by the Windows console exception. `PYTHONUTF8=1` or `-X utf8` makes `open()` default to UTF-8, but the code must pass `encoding=` explicitly anyway. `PYTHONUTF8` and `PYTHONIOENCODING` should not change any output byte if stdout is reconfigured and `open()` is always given an encoding.
30. Without a reconfigure, stderr on a Windows pipe uses the locale code page with `backslashreplace`. A path like `C:\Users\Jürgen\tx.csv` in an error message could then be written as `J\xfcrgen`, or as cp1252 bytes. Reconfigure stderr to UTF-8 too: `sys.stderr.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="backslashreplace")`. This also stops a surrogateescaped argv path from crashing the error path.
31. `-I` implies `-E`, `-P` and `-s` (docs). `python -m csvledger` puts the cwd on `sys.path` (docs). Do not run the CLI under `-I` or `-P` in tests, or `import csvledger` will fail.

**Error handling and exit codes**
32. Expected exceptions are `OSError` (including `FileNotFoundError`, `PermissionError`, and `IsADirectoryError` on POSIX), `UnicodeDecodeError`, `csv.Error`, and `re.error`. `re.error` is not the only compile failure. The probe `re.compile("a{99999999999}")` raised `OverflowError`. Catch `(re.error, OverflowError, RecursionError)` around compile.
33. The catch-all must be `except Exception` mapped to exit 1. It must not catch `SystemExit`, or argparse's exit codes of 2 and 0 would be lost. `KeyboardInterrupt` is outside the contract. `BrokenPipeError` on stdout is an `OSError`; decide its exit code. An unflushed stdout error at interpreter shutdown gives exit 120, so flush explicitly inside the `try`.
34. Windows device names such as `NUL` or `CON` can be opened as files and read as empty. They would report "missing header" and not "cannot read file". This is an edge case, and the spec can note it as undefined or accept it.

**Stdout and stderr ordering**
35. stdout is block-buffered when it is a pipe, and stderr is not. When captured separately (the normal subprocess pattern) the interleaving is unobservable. If a test merges them with `stderr=STDOUT`, order depends on flushes. To honour "warning after stdout output", call `sys.stdout.flush()` before writing the warning to stderr. On error paths write nothing to stdout.

**Testing with pytest**
36. Invoke the CLI as `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "csvledger", ...], cwd=REPO_ROOT, capture_output=True)` with `REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]`. Do not pass `text=True`. That decodes with the locale and applies universal-newline translation, which turns `\r\n` into `\n` and would mask the exact bug AC10 wants to catch. Compare raw `bytes`.
37. `<path>` in error messages is the argv string verbatim. With `cwd` at the repo root and files in `tmp_path`, the argument is an absolute path, so the expected message must be built from the same string. Exact relative-path messages like `tx.csv:3: ...` (as in O3) need `cwd=tmp_path` plus `env["PYTHONPATH"]=REPO_ROOT`. This changes sys.path ordering, but it works because `-m` still adds the cwd. Alternatively, the test can run from the repo root against a relative path to a fixture directory committed in the repo (such as `tests/fixtures/o3/tx.csv`).
38. A determinism matrix is cheap and valuable: run each case under the environment variants (`PYTHONUTF8` unset, `=0`, `=1`; `PYTHONIOENCODING` unset and `=latin-1`; `LC_ALL=C` where applicable). Assert identical bytes. Always start from a copy of `os.environ` with `PYTHONUTF8`, `PYTHONIOENCODING`, `FORCE_COLOR` and `NO_COLOR` removed.
39. `tmp_path` on Windows often contains a non-ASCII username. A test with a non-ASCII filename and description is therefore worth including, to exercise the stderr UTF-8 and `backslashreplace` handling.

- `prog="csvledger"` explicitly, on the parser; the subparsers inherit it.
- Required subcommand: `add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)`. Argparse failures exit 2. `--help` exits 0.

- Month, date, amount and priority validation must be ASCII-only (`fullmatch` with `[0-9]`, or `re.ASCII`). The contract's `\d` and `$` as written would accept Unicode digits and a trailing newline.

- Every `open()` must pass `encoding="utf-8-sig"` and `newline=""`. The read loop is inside the exception handling.
- Output is built completely before any write. Exit 3 or 4 means stdout is empty, so nothing is written until all inputs have loaded.
- Output is UTF-8 with `\n` newlines on every platform. Flush stdout before writing the duplicate warning.
- JSON empty results are the three-line indent=2 form, not `{"months": []}` on one line, unless the spec says otherwise.
- Catch `OSError`, `UnicodeDecodeError`, `csv.Error`, `re.error`/`OverflowError`/`RecursionError`, then `Exception` for exit 1. Never intercept `SystemExit`.
- Tests must compare bytes and must not run the CLI under `-I`.

1. Add a row for `csv.Error` (field too large) to the error table, or raise the field limit. State what happens for NUL bytes.
2. State what a blank line 1 means (missing header vs skipped).
3. State how table cells handle control characters (`\n`, `\r`, NUL, U+2028). Suggested: replace or escape them in table output so no cell can add a line break. Keep JSON as is.
4. State that `<line>` is the physical line at the end of the record.
5. Reconfigure stderr to UTF-8 with `errors="backslashreplace"`, in addition to the stdout reconfigure the contract already requires. Wrap both in a try/except so they tolerate replaced streams.
6. Prefer writing `sys.stdout.buffer.write(text.encode("utf-8"))` over `sys.stdout.write`.
7. State the abbreviation policy (`allow_abbrev=False` on every parser is recommended for a strict CLI), and state whether options after FILE are accepted.
8. Define the message printed for exit 1 (suggest `csvledger: error: internal error: <ExceptionType>`) and the exit code for `BrokenPipeError`.
9. State that help text stays ASCII, and that help width wrapping may depend on terminal size.
10. 11. Add a note that `from __future__` and `match` features need 3.10+, and that all stdlib calls used are available in 3.11. `tomllib` is not needed.
